body:
## Summary

`purrdf rules --srl` uses memory and time that grow **quadratically** with the data when a rule body has two `rdf:type` patterns whose subjects share no variable, even when the other patterns in the body connect them. Remove one of the two `rdf:type` patterns and the same rule runs in linear time and memory.

It looks as if the two type patterns are joined first, producing every Vault × every Spool, and only then filtered by `k:target`, which actually links them.

Found by Katamari while measuring placement admissibility as SPARQL 1.2 RL rules with `--explain` proofs. An unbounded run at 100,000 vaults used all memory on a 128 GB machine.

## Environment

- `purrdf --version`: `purrdf 3.0.1` (release build of the CLI, built 2026-10-05)
- Local checkout at `dfc0c21ad`
- Linux x86_64

## Reproduction

`gen.py` writes N vaults. Each vault has exactly three targets, one of them a spool, so the work per vault is constant:

```python
import sys
n = int(sys.argv[1])
print("@prefix k: <https://example.invalid/k#> .")
for i in range(n):
    print(f"k:v{i} a k:Vault ; k:target k:v{i}a, k:v{i}b, k:v{i}c .")
    print(f"k:v{i}a a k:Store .")
    print(f"k:v{i}b a k:Store .")
    print(f"k:v{i}c a k:Spool .")
```

`single.srl` has two `rdf:type` patterns joined through `k:target`:

```sparql
PREFIX k: <https://example.invalid/k#>
PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>
RULE { ?v k:hasSpool ?s } WHERE {
  ?v rdf:type k:Vault ; k:target ?s . ?s rdf:type k:Spool .
}
```

`notype.srl` is the same rule without `?v rdf:type k:Vault`:

```sparql
PREFIX k: <https://example.invalid/k#>
PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>
RULE { ?v k:hasSpool ?s } WHERE {
  ?v k:target ?s . ?s rdf:type k:Spool .
}
```

`pair.srl` has three type patterns, two of them on paired variables. This was the original case:

```sparql
PREFIX k: <https://example.invalid/k#>
PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>
RULE { ?v k:hasTwoSpools true } WHERE {
  ?v rdf:type k:Vault ; k:target ?s1, ?s2 .
  ?s1 rdf:type k:Spool . ?s2 rdf:type k:Spool .
  FILTER(?s1 != ?s2)
}
```

Run with:

```sh
python3 gen.py 4000 > d4000.ttl
purrdf rules --srl single.srl --max-join-steps 18446744073709551615 d4000.ttl out.nt
```

`--max-join-steps` is raised so that the default ceiling does not stop the run before the growth shows. The memory figures below come from running under a 4 GB address-space limit (`RLIMIT_AS`) and reading peak RSS with `getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN)`.

## Measurements

| vaults | rule | time | peak RSS | result |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1,000 | `single` (2 type patterns) | 0.40 s | 243 MB | ok |
| 2,000 | `single` | 1.56 s | 912 MB | ok |
| 4,000 | `single` | 5.88 s | 3,579 MB | ok |
| 1,000 | `pair` (3 type patterns) | 1.18 s | 304 MB | ok |
| 2,000 | `pair` | 4.30 s | 1,157 MB | ok |
| 4,000 | `pair` | — | > 4 GB | aborted by the 4 GB limit |
| 1,000 | `notype` (1 type pattern) | 0.07 s | 23 MB | ok |
| 4,000 | `notype` | 0.12 s | 61 MB | ok |
| 20,000 | `notype` | 0.77 s | 286 MB | ok, 20,000 inferred |

Each time the input doubles, peak memory for `single` and `pair` grows about 4×, which is quadratic. For `notype` it grows about 2×, which is linear.

## Expected

Join order should follow the shared variables, or selectivity, rather than putting two disconnected `rdf:type` patterns next to each other. With `?v` bound first and each vault reaching three targets, all three rules should be linear in the number of vaults.

## Related

Possibly worth a separate issue: the default `--max-join-steps` ceiling (1,048,576) can be raised but not removed, and when it is reached the run fails with no partial result. In Katamari's highest-assurance profile, chosen limits are not permitted, only physical ones.
title: rules: two rdf:type patterns with disjoint subjects are joined as a cross product (quadratic memory in SPARQL 1.2 RL)

body:
A regression from the exact-tower PR (#441, commit ebe79697a, "run a governed forked loop in small blocks taken in order").

Bench `governed_eval/row_loops_16384` (16,384 cheap rows), RAYON_NUM_THREADS=32, median ms:

| Lane | now | before blocks | main before #441 |
|---|---|---|---|
| filter, fuel + stop signal | 5.07 | 3.49 | 3.31 |
| bind, fuel + stop signal | 10.98 | 7.06 | 8.59 |
| filter, stop signal only | 4.18 | 3.57 | 3.38 |
| bind, stop signal only | 10.96 | 8.05 | 6.65 |

The ungoverned controls are flat (1.03–1.09×), and one thread does not regress.

Likely cause: about 2,048 blocks of 8 items at 32 threads, each with its own worker context, ledger clone, `ScratchInterner::over` and harvest. Blocks are used even when only a stop signal is present and there is no spend to share.

Required:
- use blocks only when a fuel or scratch headroom is engaged;
- set a minimum block length (or size blocks from the row count and thread count);
- re-bench this lane A/B against main. The memory bound (about one ceiling plus in-flight rows), determinism across thread counts and the exact trip points must all hold.
- Update docs/BENCHMARKS.md.

Also fix:
- **Stale doc:** the module doc in `crates/sparql-eval/src/row_checkpoint.rs` (around lines 65–76) still describes the retired per-prefix stopping rule.
- **False claim:** the CHANGELOG and the governor profile say a governed OPTIONAL filter still forks, but on the CLI it never does. The CLI's metered base engages the intermediate-cells dimension, so `cell_row_ceiling` is `Some`. Either make it fork or correct the claim. Measured on 200,000 rows at 32 threads: 0.6 s ungoverned against 3.1 s under `--fuel`.

Refs #423, #469.
title: SPARQL governor: governed parallel row loops regressed 1.2–1.65× at 32 threads (block scheduling)

body:
There must be one integer type. Main's `purrdf_xsd::bigint::BigInt` (base 1e9, from the exact numeric tower) and the binary integer the geodesy work built (`crate::integer::Int` on branch `paudley/408-geo-deterministic-geodesic-distance-in`: three limbs inline, allocation-free scratch variants) cannot coexist. Two integer types on main is not acceptable.

Replace main's base-1e9 representation with the binary integer:
- Extract the binary integer from the geodesy branch, with its zero-allocation guarantees and tests, as the workspace's only arbitrary-precision integer.
- Rebuild the exact tower's arithmetic on it: add, sub, mul (schoolbook and Karatsuba), div/rem, gcd, pow, sqrt_floor, mul_div_rem. Rebuild Integer, Decimal and Rational, and decimal parsing and printing, at the edges.
- Replace the base-1e9 cost model (`exact/cost.rs`, `limb_len`, `leading_u64`, `decimal_digits`) with binary-limb charges. Publish them as governor profile v14, with the vectors and corpus regenerated by their generators.
- Preserve everything: exact results on every surface (Rust, CLI, Python, C, wasm32, byte-identical natively and on wasm32), DivisionPolicy semantics, F&O error codes, determinism across thread counts, no over-refusal at the minimum answering ceilings, and the existing exact-tower tests, including the 100,000-row SUM/AVG oracle.
- Benches: small values must not regress against main, and large values must not regress against main's Karatsuba. Report both.

The geodesy PR (#463) then merges on top, sharing this integer, as governor profile v15. Refs #443, #423, #408.
title: xsd: one binary arbitrary-precision integer for the whole workspace

body:
Owner rule: OWL DL, RL and Full are the minimum support floor. The vendored W3C OWL 2 suite agrees on 258 of 262 cases. Four are ledgered in `crates/sparql-conformance/src/owl2.rs`:
- `new-feature-bottomdataproperty-001` and `new-feature-bottomobjectproperty-001` (BottomProperty): `owl:bottomObjectProperty` and `owl:bottomDataProperty` are read as ordinary roles, so an assertion over one does not clash.
- `webont-thing-003` (EmptyDomain): `owl:Thing owl:equivalentClass owl:Nothing` must be inconsistent, because OWL 2 forbids the empty domain.
- `webont-i5-26-007` (CyclicClassExpression): returns an EntailError rather than a verdict.

Required: all four agree with the published verdicts and leave the ledger (0 ledgered), with no new unsoundness on the RL negative lane.
title: OWL 2 DL: close the four ledgered W3C OWL 2 consistency divergences

body: Owner rule: running Java on this host is forbidden, and PurRDF exists to replace Java RDF tooling. The LUBM lane still depends on the Java UBA generator. Replace it with a deterministic Rust LUBM generator that is byte-identical for a given seed and university count, matching the UBA output's statistics and schema. Then remove every Java and JRE dependency from the scripts, tests, CI and docs.
title: Benchmarks: replace the Java LUBM generator with a deterministic Rust generator
Schema surface: remove fixed caps that refuse valid large input

body: `for v in row` over a solution row raises KeyError instead of yielding values. rdflib 7.6's ResultRow is a tuple, so iteration yields values in projection order, with None for unbound. Fix the native row and the `purrdf.compat.rdflib` row so they match that, consistently with the .pyi stubs. Test bound, unbound, empty-projection and SELECT * rows. As neighbours, indexing by name and by position, `len` and `asdict` must keep working.
title: Python: iterating a SPARQL solution row with 'for v in row' raises KeyError

body:
The Turtle renderer recurses once per nested blank-node level when it packs `[ … ]` property lists. A long blank-node chain, such as a long RDF collection built by hand or a deep `[ ex:p [ ex:p … ] ]`, can exhaust the native stack, and there is a related pack-depth limit. The owner ruled that the deep-chain guard stays permanently. What remains is to make the renderer stack-safe (an explicit work list, not recursion) and its pack-depth handling correct and deterministic.

Required: Turtle and TriG output over 10^5- and 10^6-deep blank-node chains completes natively and on wasm32, byte-identically. Shallow chains keep their packed output. Add a bench.
title: Turtle writer: deep blank-node chains recurse on the native stack

v4.0 Breaking (owner: the decimal defaults deferred to v4.0 are now due).
1. Remove the 3.x bounded Decimal and i128 numeric types. The exact tower becomes the only numeric API.
2. The default DivisionPolicy is EXACT when the quotient terminates (the reduced divisor has only the factors 2 and 5). Otherwise it keeps 18 fractional digits, rounded HALF-TO-EVEN. This replaces 3.x's default of 18 digits truncated. `exact`, `N` and `N:ROUNDING` stay available.
3. Temporal seconds are fully exact.

Cover the CLI, Rust, Python, C and wasm, the governor profile (a version bump with regenerated vectors), the CHANGELOG Breaking section and the book (with zh-Hans). Work in progress: branch `paudley/423-v4-decimal-defaults`. Refs #423.
title: v4.0: exact tower only, and an exact-or-18-half-even default division policy

| Threads | Fuel | Scratch | Metered |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.98× | 1.10× | 1.42× |

Determinism and the governor profile vectors must not change, unless the profile version is bumped with regenerated vectors.
title: SPARQL governor: metered governed evaluation costs 1.4–1.7× ungoverned (target 1.2×)

body:
The developer-schema surface admits a checked literal (node or literal, under the OWL 2 Full floor) on every OWL-derived property. Every datatype in the OWL 2 datatype map has its lexical form checked, except `rdf:XMLLiteral`: its lexical space is well-balanced XML, which no JSON Schema pattern can decide. Unconstrained cells still report `exact` while admitting any `rdf:XMLLiteral` lexical form.

Required: either judge well-balanced XML exactly (a schema keyword or a validator hook the surface can rely on), or report every cell that can hold an `rdf:XMLLiteral` truthfully as `representation_approximation`. Add tests for an ill-formed and a well-formed XMLLiteral. Refs #416.
title: Schema surface: rdf:XMLLiteral literal lexical forms are admitted unjudged
XPath regex: large finite counted repetitions are refused on 1–4 MiB input

body:
The rdflib compatibility shim (`purrdf.compat.rdflib`) handles variable reassignment with a text rewrite. A text rewrite can't reproduce rdflib 7.6's answers when a reassigned variable meets `OPTIONAL`, `MINUS`, `EXISTS`, `GROUP BY`, `SELECT *` or a nested group. In those cases the shim currently raises `UnmodelledReassignment` instead of answering.

Goal: replace the text rewrite with an algebra-level rewrite, so the shim gives exactly rdflib 7.6's answer for every reassignment, with no `UnmodelledReassignment` refusals left.

Acceptance:
- Differential tests against rdflib 7.6 cover reassignment under each of `OPTIONAL`, `MINUS`, `EXISTS`, `GROUP BY`, `SELECT *`, nested groups and their combinations. Every case matches rdflib.
- `UnmodelledReassignment` is removed, or provably unreachable.
- Every case that works today keeps its current answer.
title: rdflib shim: algebra-level reassignment rewrite so every case matches rdflib 7.6

body:
## Summary

`rdf:langString` used as a datatype is reported as an `unrecognized-term` boundary. RDF 1.2 defines `rdf:langString`, and `rdf:dirLangString` for directional language strings, as the datatypes of language-tagged literals.

## Reproduction (purrdf 3.0.0 from crates.io)

```
<http://example.org/p> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#DatatypeProperty> .
<http://example.org/p> <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#range> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#langString> .
```

Result: `true`, `decided-within-boundaries`, boundaries `{unrecognized-term}`.

## Expected

`rdf:langString` (and `rdf:dirLangString`) should be recognized datatypes whose value space is the language-tagged strings, decided exactly like `xsd:string`.

## Impact

The gmeow-ontology production class world `graph/logic` declares `rdfs:range rdf:langString` (4 uses), which contributes one of its boundaries.
title: rdf:langString ranges are reported as unrecognized-term

body:
## Summary

Any `owl:propertyChainAxiom` makes `Reasoner::consistency` report `completeness decided-within-boundaries` with a `property-chain` boundary. Chains are not part of the decided fragment in 3.0.0.

## Reproduction (purrdf 3.0.0 from crates.io)

```
<http://example.org/p> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#ObjectProperty> .
<http://example.org/q> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#ObjectProperty> .
<http://example.org/r> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#ObjectProperty> .
<http://example.org/r> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#propertyChainAxiom> _:l1 .
_:l1 <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#first> <http://example.org/p> .
_:l1 <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#rest> _:l2 .
_:l2 <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#first> <http://example.org/q> .
_:l2 <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#rest> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#nil> .
```

Result: `true`, `decided-within-boundaries`, boundaries `{property-chain}`.

## Expected

OWL 2 DL (SROIQ) admits regular role-inclusion chains (`p ∘ q ⊑ r` under the regularity condition). These should be decided exactly. A chain that violates regularity should be refused, as non-OWL 2 DL input already is.

## Impact

The gmeow-ontology production class world `graph/logic` states 9 property chains. Each one keeps that world's consistency verdict from being exact.
title: owl:propertyChainAxiom is a property-chain boundary; regular chains are not decided

body:
## Summary

`xsd:dateTimeStamp` is not exactly decided by `purrdf_xsd::range::is_exactly_decided`, so any ontology that uses it as a range makes `Reasoner::consistency` report `completeness decided-within-boundaries` with a `data-range` boundary. `xsd:dateTime` and `xsd:date` decide exactly.

## Reproduction (purrdf 3.0.0 from crates.io)

```
<http://example.org/p> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#DatatypeProperty> .
<http://example.org/p> <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#range> <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#dateTimeStamp> .
```

`Reasoner::new(&dataset)?.consistency()` with the range set to each datatype:

| range | answer | completeness | boundaries |
|---|---|---|---|
| `xsd:dateTimeStamp` | true | decided-within-boundaries | `data-range` |
| `xsd:dateTime` | true | decided | none |
| `xsd:date` | true | decided | none |
| `xsd:integer` | true | decided | none |

## Expected

`xsd:dateTimeStamp` is an OWL 2 datatype: `xsd:dateTime` restricted to values with a timezone (`explicitTimezone = required`). Its value space is a subset of `xsd:dateTime`'s, which is already decided exactly. The range should be decided exactly, with no boundary.

## Impact

This is the only boundary that the gmeow-ontology production class world `graph/imports` raises. That world declares `rdfs:range xsd:dateTimeStamp` on two properties. Because of the boundary, that world's consistency verdict can never be exact, whatever the reasoner's speed.
title: xsd:dateTimeStamp ranges are not exactly decided (data-range boundary)

body:
## Goal

Make the exact numeric tower (`purrdf_xsd::exact::{Integer, Decimal, Rational}`, added in #441) at least as fast as the bounded types for in-range values, and competitive with dedicated bignum libraries for large ones. The tower becomes the default numeric path once #441 lands, so its speed is query speed.

This is separate from #441 on purpose: #441 keeps in-range values on the existing bounded fast path, so it ships with no regression. This issue is about making the tower itself fast.

## Measured starting point

Instructions per operation on small values, from #441's `crates/xsd/benches/exact.rs`:

| Operation | Exact tower | Bounded |
|---|---:|---:|
| integer `+` | 49.7 | 66.4 |
| integer `×` | 78.0 | 95.4 |
| decimal `+` | 138.7 | 131.2 |
| decimal `×` | 158.9 | 105.4 |
| decimal `÷` | 346.5 | 231.7 |
| decimal parse + render | 1,469 | 1,459 |
| decimal → `f64` | 100.4 | 97.8 |

For large values, addition, parse and render scale linearly from 40 to 40,000 digits. Multiplication uses Karatsuba above 64 limbs; the threshold came from an instruction-count sweep. Division costs quotient length × divisor length.

## Scope

1. **Small-value decimal `×`/`÷`:** reach parity with bounded or better. The likely cause is canonicalising (stripping trailing zeros) after every operation. Try lazy canonicalisation, normalising only at render, compare, hash and equality.
2. **Use the tower wherever it wins:** integer `+` and `×` are already faster than bounded. Measure end-to-end in the SPARQL evaluator, and switch the in-range hybrid path per operation wherever the tower wins.
3. **Large multiplication:** Toom-3 (and possibly Toom-4) above the Karatsuba range, with an FFT or NTT-based multiply for very large operands. Tune each threshold by an instruction-count sweep on native and wasm32.
4. **Large division:** Burnikel–Ziegler recursive division, or Newton reciprocal division, so division costs about the same as multiplication.
5. **Decimal ↔ string:** subquadratic radix conversion (divide-and-conquer with cached powers of ten) for parse and render past a few hundred digits.
6. **SIMD:** limb loops (add/sub carry chains, schoolbook inner loop) on x86_64-v3/v4, aarch64 NEON and wasm32 simd128, wherever `make simd-asm` shows they vectorize or can be written to. Each new kernel needs a portable reference, a goldens test and a `scripts/simd-asm-manifest.toml` site.
7. **Allocation:** cut allocations for medium values, for example inline storage for 2–4 limbs and reusing scratch buffers in division, and prove the reduction with the alloc probes.
8. **Rational:** cheaper GCD reduction (binary or Lehmer GCD) and fewer reductions in chained operations.

## Constraints

- **Exactness:** results stay exact and bit-identical across native and wasm32. The `purrdf_testkit::exact` oracle properties and the wasm determinism digest must still pass.
- **Governor:** cost estimates (`exact::Cost`) must keep bounding the real work after every algorithm change, without over-refusing. A cost must never under-report.
- **Benches:** every change needs a bench row (`purrdf_testkit::bench`, `docs/BENCHMARKS.md`, `docs/design/purrdf-simd.md`). Measure with instructions:u, not wall time.
- **Dependencies:** no new external dependency without approval. The tower is first-party by design.

## Acceptance

- Every row in the table above is at parity with bounded or better.
- Large-value curves show the new asymptotics (Toom, subquadratic division and radix conversion), with sweep-tuned thresholds recorded.
- Before/after tables for the SPARQL arithmetic, ORDER BY, SUM/AVG and FILTER lanes, with no regression anywhere.
title: Optimize the exact numeric tower: small-value parity and subquadratic large-value arithmetic

body:
Radius and box search over point literals needs a hierarchical cell index: each
point is keyed by the cell that contains it at a fixed resolution, and a query
covers its region with a set of cells and refines by exact distance. `purrdf-geo`
has no cell index, so a consumer doing this keeps a third-party hexagonal-grid
library beside purrdf, and the cell ids it stores are only as stable as that
library's version.

## Ask

A deterministic hierarchical spatial cell index in `purrdf-geo` for CRS84 points:

- **Cell assignment:** point (longitude, latitude) and resolution to a cell id, a
  pure function of its inputs, identical on every host and target (no floating
  point that a platform `libm` can move; exact or fixed-point arithmetic, or a
  declared, tested rounding contract).
- **Parent / children** across resolutions, so a cell can be coarsened (for
  example to bound disclosure precision) or refined.
- **Covering:** the set of cells at a resolution that covers a disk of a given
  radius in metres (paired with the geodesic distance requested separately) and a
  bounding box, with a declared, finite bound on the cover size and a typed refusal
  past it rather than a silently truncated cover.
- **Range checks:** latitude outside [-90, 90] or longitude outside [-180, 180]
  refused with a typed error; never assigned a plausible cell.
- **Identity:** the grid and its parameters named in a versioned profile, so a
  change re-mints the identity of every index built on it.

H3 compatibility (same cell ids as the H3 reference) would be welcome but is not
required; determinism and a stable, versioned definition are.

## Acceptance

- Conformance vectors for assignment, parent/child, and covering, including the
  poles, the antimeridian, and resolution extremes.
- The cover of a radius contains every cell that holds a point within the radius
  (no false negatives), checked exhaustively on small radii.
- Out-of-range coordinates refuse.
title: geo: deterministic hierarchical spatial cell index for CRS84 points (assignment, parent/child, covering)

body:
`purrdf-geo` registers the ellipsoidal geodesic needed by the `geof:metric*` family
but hard-errors on it by name, and `measure::distance` is an exact planar distance
in the coordinate reference system's own units. A consumer that ranks or filters
points on WGS84 by distance in metres therefore has to carry its own great-circle
computation beside purrdf.

## Ask

A deterministic geodesic distance in metres between two points in OGC CRS84
(longitude, latitude), exposed both as a Rust function and through the
`geof:metric*` functions that currently hard-error:

- the WGS84 ellipsoid geodesic (Karney's algorithm), with a declared tolerance; and/or
- a spherical great-circle (haversine) variant on a declared mean radius, under its
  own name so the two are never confused;
- out-of-range latitude or longitude refused with a typed error rather than
  wrapped or clamped;
- a stated rounding contract, so two hosts given the same coordinates return the
  same value.

## Acceptance

- Conformance vectors against published geodesic test data (for example Karney's
  GeodTest set) within the declared tolerance.
- Antipodal and near-antipodal pairs, the poles, and the antimeridian are covered.
- The functions that hard-error today return metres instead.
title: geo: deterministic geodesic distance in metres for CRS84 (geof:metric*)

body:
## Problem
XSD/XPath regular expressions in SPARQL, SHACL and ShEx do not follow a dated XPath grammar or its matching rules, such as XPath 3.1 backreferences, non-capturing groups and the `q` flag. Errors also do not separate syntax failures (which may become expression errors or UNDEF) from resource refusals (which must stay operational errors).

## Proposed solution
Design a native XPath regex profile with:
- explicit profile selection
- finite VM limits
- operational resource refusal, including a distinct error for oversized patterns rather than a syntax error
- Unicode data from the generator only

JSON Schema ECMA matching must keep its current engine behaviour; any shared VM must not turn previously accepted patterns into resource errors. All public changes are additive (no new variants on closed enums).

## Acceptance
- Grammar and matching conformance vectors per profile.
- Resource-limit tests checking that limits surface as operational errors, not syntax errors.
- No behaviour change in JSON Schema.
- `cargo semver-checks`, `make check` and `make wasm` pass.
title: Native XPath regex profile with operational resource refusal

body:
## Problem
SHACL validation has no explicit profile selection between SHACL 1.0 (REC 2017) and the SHACL 1.2 drafts. The report also cannot carry everything required:
- `sh:sourceConstraint`
- the normative message precedence
- blank-node identity of report contexts

`ValidationResult` is a public struct without `#[non_exhaustive]`, so these cannot be added as new fields. The SPARQL pre-binding admission policy (VALUES / MINUS / SERVICE / hidden pre-bound subquery variables) is one fixed policy instead of one per profile.

## Proposed solution
- Add a profile selector and a richer report door, both additive. The default profile and existing report types stay unchanged.
- Make the pre-binding admission rules depend on the selected profile, with required-rejection tests for constructs the profile forbids.
- Wire the SHACL cases of the community corpus into the community conformance runner, reporting unsupported profiles separately from failures.

## Acceptance
- Exact report comparison: graph isomorphism plus the required fields.
- Every refusal is paired with a valid neighbouring case that still validates.
- Python and wasm expectations stay unchanged under the default profile.
- `cargo semver-checks` passes for shapes and validate.
title: SHACL dated profile selection and complete validation reports (additive)

body:
## Problem
1. `LOAD` merges blank nodes across independent documents. Parsers put every blank node in the default blank scope, and `load()` inserts the values without remapping, so two LOADs that both contain `_:b0` share one node. RDF semantics requires each document's blank nodes to be kept apart, including those inside nested triple terms.
2. ADD/COPY/MOVE move records through a projection that flattens the three RDF 1.2 statement surfaces (ordinary, reifier, annotation) and then reclassifies them on insert, so a transfer can lose or change a record's role.

## Proposed solution
- Give each loaded document its own blank-node remapping, reusing the existing blank-node counter and handling nested triple terms and CDT-embedded blank nodes.
- Make transfers typed: add record kinds/values so a reifier or annotation record stays a reifier or annotation. Public API changes must be purely additive.

## Acceptance
Failing-first Rust tests: two LOADs of `_:b0` stay distinct; nested-term blank nodes stay consistent within a document and separate across documents; reifier and annotation roles survive ADD, COPY and MOVE in both graph-existence modes. `cargo semver-checks`, `make check` and `make wasm` pass.
title: Update transfers preserve RDF 1.2 identity: per-document LOAD blank scoping and typed record transfer

body:
## Problem

PurRDF passed its frozen W3C corpora while SHACL-SPARQL pre-binding could produce a false `conforms=true` result (#382). Our current W3C SHACL and first-party query fixtures have no `OPTIONAL` groups; left-hand focus-node anchors masked the failing interaction. The named-graph work (#383) also shows the value of testing graph isolation and measuring adapter costs independently of semantic correctness.

Build a portable community conformance extension and contribute missing normative cases to the official W3C suites. The 3.0.1 fixes remain owned by #382/#383/#385; this issue owns the reusable corpus, coverage method and upstream contribution.

## Proposed solution

Publish small RDF data/shapes/query fixtures with W3C-compatible manifests, expected results, stable test identifiers, versioned provenance and reusable licensing. Each expected result must have an independently reviewed specification rationale; PurRDF output and agreement between engines are evidence, not the oracle. Compare reports by the applicable normative requirements and graph isomorphism, allowing variations the specification explicitly permits.

Start with a coverage matrix for SHACL pre-binding: empty-left and nested `OPTIONAL`; `EXISTS`/`NOT EXISTS`; unions, paths and legal subqueries/modifiers; IRI and blank-node identity; predicate positions; constraints, ASK/SELECT validators and SPARQL rules. Include both conforming and violating data plus controls that expose incorrect outer-join-only binding. Tag SHACL 1.0, SHACL 1.2 draft revisions and AF/RDF 1.2 cases explicitly. Constructs forbidden by a profile, including SHACL 1.0 `MINUS`, `SERVICE`, explicit `VALUES` and hidden pre-bound subquery variables, belong in required-rejection tests for that profile.

Add the SPARQL interactions exposed by #385: alternatives of predicates, inverse and sequence arms; overlapping arms and duplicate solution multiplicities; hidden intermediate variables; and equivalent UNION/group-pattern permutations. Review exact result bags against SPARQL 1.1 algebra independently of planner behavior. Retain scaled execution/admission regressions in the implementation and benchmark companion: a particular resource budget or timing threshold is not a W3C normative requirement.

Use the same portable fixtures across native and prepared execution and applicable language bindings. Run PurRDF and at least two independent engines with pinned versions and recorded capabilities. Triaged disagreements must retain the fixture and normative rationale; unsupported profiles must be reported distinctly from passes. Export reproducible EARL reports.

Maintain a benchmark companion for selected-graph validation: native views, generic composition and materialization; graph size/source count; shape-only class supplementation; RDF 1.2 statement overlays; preparation time, lookup/validation time and memory. Require equivalent validation reports and reproducible inputs. Hardware-specific timing and PurRDF API/allocation contracts remain benchmark or adapter results, separate from W3C conformance claims.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publish the coverage matrix, including each category's cases and specification/profile references.
- [ ] Extract and expand the hotfix regressions into standalone portable fixtures with independently reviewed expected outcomes.
- [ ] Demonstrate that the false-conformance cases fail the old behavior and pass the corrected implementation; retain positive and negative controls.
- [ ] Provide reproducible cross-engine runs, pinned versions, capability declarations, triaged differences and EARL reports.
- [ ] Integrate all applicable community cases into PurRDF's conformance gate with strict unexpected-pass/failure discipline; preserve the frozen upstream corpora and their provenance.
- [ ] Publish the report-equivalent benchmark companion with its methods and measured limits.
- [ ] Prepare and submit upstream test PRs using W3C manifests and `sht:proposed` status; incorporate review and track Working Group decisions without labeling pending proposals approved.
- [ ] Document standalone use, licensing/provenance and contribution instructions so other implementers can run and extend the corpus.

## References

- [SPARQL property-path translation and multiset algebra](https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql11-query/#sparqlTranslatePathPatterns).
- [SHACL pre-binding definition and query restrictions](https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/#pre-binding).
- [W3C SHACL test format, proposed-test process and EARL reporting](https://w3c.github.io/data-shapes/data-shapes-test-suite/).
- [Existing W3C request to extend suite coverage](https://github.com/w3c/data-shapes/issues/190).
- [W3C contribution requirements](https://github.com/w3c/data-shapes/blob/gh-pages/CONTRIBUTING.md).
title: Build a portable adversarial SHACL suite and contribute missing W3C tests

body:
## Goal

Replace the retained `sha2` crate with a native `purrdf_hash::sha2` that is **faster than `sha2` on the backend dispatch selects, on every architecture we can measure**, and correct on every other backend. When that bar is met, `sha2` leaves every manifest. The ban goes on `BANNED_ANY_EDGE` once no transitive holder remains.

## Why it is still `sha2` today

A native implementation was built and benchmarked against `sha2` 0.11.0 while centralizing helpers (#366, [bench record](https://github.com/Blackcat-Informatics/purrdf/issues/366#issuecomment-5882732813)). It was discarded because it did not beat `sha2`.

Method: Zen 5 host (SHA-NI, AVX-512, no SHA512 extensions); native and `sha2` interleaved in one process in ABBA order; 601 pairs per cell; bootstrap 95% CI on the difference of medians.

| cell | native vs sha2 |
|---|---|
| SHA-256 SHA-NI 64 B | −3.7% (faster) |
| SHA-256 SHA-NI 1 KiB | +1.4% (slower) |
| SHA-256 SHA-NI 1 MiB | +0.04% (tie) |
| SHA-512 portable 64 B / 1 KiB / 1 MiB | +47% / +43% / +44% (slower) |

What the numbers mean:
- **Single-stream SHA-256 on SHA-NI is latency-bound.** The rounds are one serial `sha256rnds2` chain, so a single-message kernel can at best tie `sha2`. Beating it needs a different *shape* of work, not a better copy of the same loop.
- **SHA-512 lost on the message schedule and the scalar rounds.** On this host `sha2` computes the SHA-512 schedule with AVX2. The native portable rounds also lost to `sha2`'s scalar backend by 22–47%.

## Where SHA-2 is hot in PurRDF (what "optimal" should optimize)

1. **RDFC-1.0 canonicalization** (`rdf-core/src/ir/canon.rs` `digest_hex` / `hash_lines`).
   - It runs one SHA-256 per blank node in Hash First Degree Quads, and more per round in Hash N-Degree Quads.
   - These are **many short, independent messages** (tens to hundreds of bytes). This is the hottest SHA-2 path.
2. **Bulk digests**, which are throughput-bound:
   - `sink::Digest` (streaming document digests);
   - `ContentDigest::of`;
   - embedding section digests;
   - pack and artifact certification.
3. **Cold paths**, once per query or artifact: query provenance, the governor schedule digest, slice cache keys, `gts_certify`, and the SPARQL `SHA256()`/`SHA384()`/`SHA512()` built-ins (these run per row, but only when a query calls them).

## Approaches with a real chance of winning

- **Multi-buffer SHA-256 for RDFC.** Hash 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX-512) independent messages in parallel lanes. That turns a latency-bound workload into a throughput-bound one, which single-stream SHA-NI cannot match. It needs a batch API (`Sha256::digest_many` or similar) and a canonicalizer that submits its per-blank-node hashes as a batch.
- **Interleaved SHA-NI.** Run 2–4 independent SHA-NI streams interleaved to hide `sha256rnds2` latency. This also serves the batch API on SHA-NI hosts.
- **SHA-512 with a vector message schedule.** Use AVX2/AVX-512 (and NEON on aarch64) for the schedule, with a register-rotating scalar round core that uses `rorx`/BMI2 where available. Where the hardware has them, add dedicated kernels for the x86 SHA512 extensions (`vsha512rnds2`) and the ARMv8.2 SHA512 instructions.
- **Single-message SHA-256 on SHA-NI:** at minimum, match `sha2`. The win comes from the batch paths above.

## Constraints

- **Provenance:** write the implementation from FIPS 180-4 and the Intel/Arm ISA documentation. No third-party implementation source may be copied. Record the provenance in `crates/hash/PROVENANCE.md`, and run a verbatim-overlap check against `sha2` before merge.
- **Dispatch:** runtime selection through `purrdf_hash::Backend`. Register every accelerated path under `PURRDF_REQUIRE_SIMD_PATHS` so CI proves it actually ran.
- **Portability:** wasm32 builds must work (portable; simd128 multi-buffer where it helps).
- **No local emulators or system software.** A kernel the development host cannot execute must be proved there by compilation, the asm audit (`scripts/simd-asm-manifest.toml` sites for the required mnemonics), and a scalar model of each instruction. The existing `aarch64` and `avx512-sde` CI jobs must execute it.
- **RDFC byte identity is preserved.** Output bytes and all published identities are unchanged; this is a speed-only change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `purrdf_hash::sha2::{Sha224, Sha256, Sha384, Sha512}` implements `purrdf_hash::Digest`, plus a batch/multi-buffer API.
- [ ] Correctness on every backend:
  - NIST CAVP short-message, long-message and Monte Carlo vectors;
  - a frozen differential against `sha2`, recorded before removal (every length 0..=256, plus 1 MiB messages);
  - streaming split at every boundary 0..=129;
  - `Backend::all_available()` equivalence;
  - wasm32 through the wasm test runner.
- [ ] The **beat bar**, on every measurable architecture's selected backend (x86_64 host; aarch64 via the CI benchmark job):
  - native median faster than `sha2` with a bootstrap 95% CI excluding 0;
  - cells: SHA-256 and SHA-512 at 64 B, 1 KiB and 1 MiB;
  - plus an **RDFC workload cell**: canonicalizing a blank-node-heavy dataset end to end, using the batch API.
  - A tie is not a pass.
- [ ] `[[site]]` rows `hash.sha256-compress` / `hash.sha512-compress` (and the multi-buffer kernels) replace `sha2.sha256-compress`, covering the same configurations and mnemonics. `make simd-asm` passes on all seven configurations.
- [ ] RDFC canonicalization uses the batch API. The W3C RDFC test suite passes and output bytes are unchanged.
- [ ] Every first-party `sha2::` use is re-pointed, and `sha2` is removed from all manifests.
  - Ban it direct-only while `ed25519-dalek` still holds it.
  - Ban it on `BANNED_ANY_EDGE` once the native Ed25519 lands.
  - The `sha2` row in `helpers-ledger.toml` becomes the native home.
- [ ] Record the benchmark results in `docs/benchmarks/` and cite them in the PR.

If the beat bar is not met on some architecture, `sha2` stays for that path. The acceptance decision is the benchmark, not effort spent.
title: perf(hash): native SHA-2 that beats the sha2 crate — multi-buffer RDFC hashing and wide-schedule SHA-512

body:
Follow-ups from finalizing the asynchronous Wasm SERVICE/LOAD work for 3.0. None of these is a breaking change or a wrong answer; each was triaged as safe to ship in 3.0 and fixable in a 3.x release.

## Asynchronous lane and the JavaScript package

- **A hung handler can outlive its deadline in Node.** The runtime arms a job's deadline with `AbortSignal.timeout`, which Node does not count as keeping the event loop alive. A `resolveService`/`resolveLoad` handler that never settles and does no I/O, with `deadlineMs` set, lets the process exit ("Detected unsettled top-level await") instead of the job rejecting with its deadline. With anything else keeping the loop alive, the deadline trips as documented. Arm the deadline so it keeps the loop alive while a job waits on a host effect.
- **Poison errors carry no `error.code`.** Once the instance is poisoned, the error a caller receives ("the wasm instance trapped … cannot be used again") has no `code`, although every other error the package throws carries its stable code as `error.code`. Give it one.
- **The two lanes' stack depth and refusal wording differ slightly.** Both lanes refuse a too-deep request with `native-sparql-evaluation-stack-exhausted`, but each spends a little stack on its own frames, so the deepest request each evaluates can differ by a few levels, and the construct the message names is whichever frame found the stack low. Measure both lanes' budget from the shared `Operation::execute` entry (and name the construct position-independently) so the two lanes agree exactly; bench the synchronous path before moving it onto governed dispatch.
- **Deep nesting under the host-stack budget is reported as a 500.** Some deeply nested shapes (OPTIONAL, EXISTS, GRAPH, MINUS, LATERAL, SERVICE at 10⁴–10⁵ levels) pass admission and are refused during evaluation with `native-sparql-evaluation-stack-exhausted`, which the Cloudflare adapter answers with 500, while the docs describe nesting past the host-stack budget as refused before evaluation with `native-sparql-host-stack-exhausted` (400). Either admit those shapes against the budget before evaluation, or map the evaluation-stack refusal to 400 and say so.
- **One JavaScript test takes about 12 minutes.** `async-concurrency.test.mjs`'s "a request as deep as the synchronous lane evaluates … frames that never poll included" runs a deep tree with `yieldEveryPolls: 0`, about 673 000 polls, each a `setTimeout(0)` turn that Node clamps to at least 1 ms. Keep the proof and cut its cost (a smaller tree that still exceeds a frame that never polls, or a larger quantum).

## Parsing and serialization cost

- **`SELECT *` over many nested sub-SELECTs that each bind a new variable parses in quadratic time and memory.** Each `SELECT *` lists every variable visible below it, so 8 000 such levels take about 26 s and 547 MiB natively. The request is refused with a typed error on wasm, but the work before the refusal grows with the square of the depth. Represent a `SELECT *` projection without materializing each level's variable list, or admit the projection size before building it.
- **The GTS writer's identity keys cost time proportional to the term count times the nesting depth**, from its per-term expansion and linear path check; a triple-term chain thousands deep writes slowly. Memoize each term's identity key as the segment union now memoizes mapped terms.
title: Post-v3.0: asynchronous Wasm lane and parse/serialize follow-ups from #358

body:
Follow-on work identified while finishing #356 (PR #360). None of it is a regression introduced there. Each item is either additive, a limit that already existed on `main`, or a refusal that is already typed.

## Evaluation limits

1. **The join-step default refuses ordinary entailment input.** Join steps grow linearly, at about 124 per triple for RDFS (5k triples → 628,222; 10k → 1,248,222; 30k → 3,728,222).
   - At the 1,048,576 default, `reason --regime rdfs` refuses any graph above roughly 8,400 triples, even one with no schema. `owl-rl` is refused at 20k.
   - The default stays at 2^20 because a rule body's candidate solutions for a round are materialised before the limit is checked, so a Cartesian body could exhaust memory first.
   - Fix the root cause: check the limit while enumerating candidates, not after. Then re-measure and raise the native default.
   - The limits can now be set on every host; this item is about the default and the enumeration.
2. **The 16 MiB term-arena ceiling (`MAX_TERM_ARENA_BYTES`) is fixed and cannot be set on any host.** It counts the input's own terms. Example: a 100k-triple, 26 MB N-Triples file with ~200-character literals is refused by `reason --regime rdfs` (`TermArenaBytes: … 23379387 term arena byte(s)`) and by `rules`. Make it a fifth caller-settable limit, with per-target defaults like the other four, on CLI, Python, wasm and C.

## Host parity (additive)

3. **Missing validate options.**
   - Python `Shapes(...)`, `Shapes.validate_nt`, `PreparedShapes.validate_nt` and `validate_store_changes` take no `conformance_disallows`.
   - wasm `shaclValidateChangesToSarif` takes neither `conformanceDisallows` nor `subClassOfInShapesGraph`.
   - Both can be added as optional trailing arguments without breaking anything.

## SHACL behaviour

4. **The `sh:ask` / `sh:select` cross-check only runs on the candidate path.** For a `sh:SPARQLTarget` carrying both, a disagreement is refused only on `validate_focus_nodes` / `validate_focus_node_ids`, which no host reaches. A whole validation enumerates the SELECT and never runs the ASK, so a contradictory target validates without complaint. Proposal: during a whole validation, also run the ASK for each SELECT result, refuse any disagreement with `SparqlTargetDisagreement`, and expose the check on every host.
5. **The subquery pre-binding refusal cites the wrong spec and is inconsistent.**
   - A CONSTRUCT whose WHERE holds a subquery that does not project `$this` is refused, citing "SHACL 1.2 SPARQL Extensions, Appendix A". Appendix A in 1.2 lists only MINUS, VALUES and `AS`, and the 1.2 suite dropped `pre-binding-006`; only the SHACL 1.0 suite requires the refusal.
   - A top-level `{ SELECT … }` body is not refused, because of the outer-projection exemption in `prebinding.rs` `check_query_body`.
   - Decide which spec governs, correct the citation, and make the two shapes consistent.
6. **Valid SPARQL solution modifiers are refused.** `ASK … LIMIT 1`, `ASK … GROUP BY … HAVING`, `DESCRIBE … LIMIT 1` and `CONSTRUCT … GROUP BY ?s` all get "unsupported SPARQL construct", although the SPARQL grammar allows them. Implement them. The refusal is typed and predates #356.

## Output polish

7. **Internal blank-node labels leak into CLI text.** The CLI prints diagnostics and rule errors with engine-internal labels (`_:gts_0000…`), while the same run's report and SARIF use `_:sg0`-style report labels. Render the report labels in stderr lines and error messages too.
title: Post-v3.0: evaluation limits, host-parity additions and SHACL/SPARQL follow-ons from #356

body:
The native workspace test lane spends most of its elapsed time compiling and preparing test artifacts. Profile and reduce that work while preserving the full gate.

Observed on final head `839e968a509246d6fc00d17d5fd9496eac8fa3e5` in [the native CI job](https://github.com/Blackcat-Informatics/purrdf/actions/runs/34911560124/job/104199963497):

- The job ran from 00:03:32 to 00:36:12 UTC on 2026-09-15, about 32 minutes 40 seconds.
- Cargo reported 26 minutes 2 seconds to finish the optimized test build.
- `crates/rdf-capi/tests/c_smoke.rs` then took 275.71 seconds. That test invokes a separate `cargo build -p purrdf-capi --profile dev` to produce a fresh shared library before compiling, linking, and running its C callers. Its measured duration includes all of those steps; their individual costs still need profiling.
- The complete native suite passed, as did the other CI lanes.

Start with Cargo timing data and separate compilation, linking, and test execution costs. Check whether repeated compilation or artifact preparation contributes materially before selecting a change.

Acceptance:

- Record comparable cold and warm phase timings before and after the change, using the configured runner concurrency.
- Keep the complete Rust suite, strict lint and hygiene gates, optimized development profile, debug assertions, and overflow checks.
- Keep the real C header, linkage, and execution checks. Any artifact reuse must prove that it matches the current sources and build configuration; file existence alone is insufficient.

This is authorized performance work to track separately from the 2.0 release. The current release continues through its existing gates without performance changes.
title: Reduce native CI test compilation and C smoke time

body:
Phases beyond the shipped entry path, per the ratified assessment `docs/design/i18n-zh-assessment.md` §7 (magnitudes are its):

- **Phase 2 — SPARQL extensions and retrieval** (~24,000 words, **large**): `sparql/querying.md` (a third of the book; holds 22 of the gated SPARQL fences), `sparql/results.md`, the text/cdt/geo crate READMEs, the embedding-kNN and text-scoring design docs, reader-facing `docs/PURREMB.md`.
- **Phase 3 — Python API guide** (~24,500 source words, **large**): a Chinese guide hosted in the book, derived from the `.pyi` comments and the PyO3 rustdoc behind `__doc__`; NOT a second `.pyi` (no locale mechanism exists in Python tooling); gate must diff the two signature lists so it cannot drift from the stub.
- **Phase 4 — remainder of the book** (~27,000 words, **large**): entailment, validation, remaining concepts, datalog/gts/slices, project pages; `entailment-rules.md` rides the gettext fallback.
- **Phase 5 — runtime strings**: recommended AGAINST as a doc phase; it is a multi-release code project (locale mechanism for clap help, 139 diagnostic sites with test-pinned messages, 269 Display impls). The shipped compromise is the Chinese diagnostic-code reference page (91 codes, already in Phase 1).

Standing rules: the vetting protocol (blind back-translation + native-reader review, all findings glossed in English) on every phase; the glossary gate is the arbiter of renderings; every stale English found while translating is fixed in English too, never silently in one language.
title: Chinese translation phases 2–4: SPARQL extensions, Python API guide, remainder of the book

PR #249 landed most of the second adversarial review's residuals, but the reviewer's list included cases worth a final pass now that real `msgstr`s are coming (issue on the pour is filed separately):

- Anchored substring collisions inside an anchored paragraph beyond the three lookarounds added (`输出处理` under provenance, `决定性能` under determinism were fixed; sweep for new ones as the glossary grows — the reviewer's method: scan every English paragraph containing an anchor for Chinese renderings that embed a rejected string).
- An anchor that appears only in a link URL of the `msgid` (should not anchor the row).
- `research 对象 (Research Object)` acceptance is house-typography-dependent; confirm the half-width-paren form matches policy or document the refusal.
- K-survival is whole-token since #249; add a self-test case per K row so a regression is caught row-by-row.

All are prevention — zero collisions existed in the book at review time. Small, self-contained, gate-only.
